The article title 'Extradigital Glomus Tumor of Thigh' supports the extradigital subtype and thigh body site. No skin, ethnicity, or age information is provided, so those fields are null/unknown. in_text_mentions: , well-defined, and oval-shaped mass (diameter, 3 mm) was identified in a branch of the cephalic vein (Figure 2). The mass was carefully resected from the vascular structure, and the vein was then ligated. Histologic examination confirmed that the mass was a glomus tumor, appearing as uniformly rounded cells with centrally located round nuclei and capillary size vessels surrounding the mass. Peripherally, the tumor was contiguous to the smooth muscle layer of the affected cephalic vein. Immunohistochemical staining revealed that the tumor cells were positive for smooth muscle actin (Figure 3).

Physical examination revealed a well-defined, smooth, purple papule 8 mm in diameter (Figure 1). Polarized, non-contact dermoscopy showed a structureless purple area (Figure 2). An excisional biopsy was performed. Histopathology confirmed the diagnosis, showing a tumor enveloped by a fibrous capsule with vascular spaces surrounded by glomus cells (Figure 3). The excision was followed by immediate disappearance of the pain without recurrence to this day.

The patient was asymptomatic and his past medical history included an orthopaedic surgery and bilateral inguinal hernia repair before seven and two years, respectively. His physical examination, his vital signs, and the laboratory studies were normal. Computed tomography (CT) identified a lesion of the right upper posterior mediastinum at the level of T3 (Figure 2(a)). CT guided biopsy was inconclusive. Differential diagnosis included mainly neurogenic origin tumors.

ient underwent a right posterolateral thoracotomy through the 5th intercostal space. A well-circumscribed vascular lesion was resected en bloc with macroscopically clear margins. The right thoracic cavity was drained by a single chest tube 32F. The patient made an uneventful postoperative recovery and he was discharged on the fifth postoperative day. Pathology report showed a benign glomus tumor of the mediastinum measuring 4.5 × 4 × 2.5 cm, with clear resection margins (Figure 2(b)). The patient, 16 months after surgery, remained in an excellent clinical status with no evidence of recurrence.

panels.attribution_text: Song et al. Gastric Glomus Tumor with Neuroendocrine Features: A Diagnostic Pitfall for Neuroendocrine Tumors.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2025. doi:10.3390/diagnostics15222865. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: On microscopic examination, Hematoxylin and Eosin staining shows tumor cells infiltrating between bundles of the muscularis propria, forming large and small islands with peripheral trabecular arrangements that could mimic a neuroendocrine tumor (NET). Numerous interspersed blood vessels and occasional calcified nodules are present. No necrosis is seen, and mitotic figures are absent (<1/50 high-power fields) (×10, H&E). (A) Tumor cells have moderate cytoplasm and relatively distinct cell borders. Nuclei are uniformly round with finely dispersed chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and regular spacing. (×200, H&E). Inset: tumor cells with round nuclei and well-defined borders (×400, H&E). (B) Immunohistochemistry shows diffuse strong positivity for smooth muscle actin (×200). We observed that 80% of central and peripheral tumor cells were weakly positive for Synaptophysin (×200). Fewer than 5% of peripheral tumor cells were weakly positive for CD56 nest (×200, CD56). Staining for Chromogranin A, CD117, and HMB-45 was negative. Gastric glomus tumors are uncommon mesenchymal neoplasms, representing about 1% of gastric mesenchymal tumors [1,2]. They typically present as submucosal masses and may closely mimic gastric neuroendocrine tumor (NET) or gastrointestinal stromal tumors. Small biopsy specimens can be misleading because glomus tumors often show small round cells forming trabecular nests, a pattern that overlaps with NET [3,4,5,6]. Immunohistochemistry is therefore critical. Synaptophysin, a standard NET marker, is positive in roughly 20% of gastric glomus tumors [7], occasionally leading to a provisional NET diagnosis when only limited small tissue is sampled [3]. We report a 60-year-old woman with a 2.5 cm antral subepithelial lesion resected laparoscopically. Histology revealed uniform round cells within the muscularis propria and abundant vasculature. Immunostaining showed strong diffuse smooth muscle actin (SMA) positivity, weak synaptophysin expression in ~80% of tumor cells, focal CD56 positivity, and negativity for CD117 and chromogranin A—features diagnostic of gastric glomus tumor. A review of 16 English-language cases of synaptophysin-positive gastric glomus tumors (including this case) shows that most are present in the antrum, affect patients aged 38–73 years, and consistently express SMA [8,9,10,11]. CD56 is rarely reported and typically weak or peripheral. Because NETs more often arise in the gastric body or fundus [6], antral location and strong SMA positivity are key differentiators for diagnosing gastric glomus tumors. Pathologists should consider SMA staining when a gastric submucosal biopsy shows round cells with well-defined borders and weak synaptophysin or peripheral CD56 expression to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment for malignancy.

Staining for Chromogranin A, CD117, and HMB-45 was negative. Gastric glomus tumors are uncommon mesenchymal neoplasms, representing about 1% of gastric mesenchymal tumors [1,2]. They typically present as submucosal masses and may closely mimic gastric neuroendocrine tumor (NET) or gastrointestinal stromal tumors. Small biopsy specimens can be misleading because glomus tumors often show small round cells forming trabecular nests, a pattern that overlaps with NET [3,4,5,6]. Immunohistochemistry is therefore critical. Synaptophysin, a standard NET marker, is positive in roughly 20% of gastric glomus tumors [7], occasionally leading to a provisional NET diagnosis when only limited small tissue is sampled [3]. We report a 60-year-old woman with a 2.5 cm antral subepithelial lesion resected laparoscopically. Histology revealed uniform round cells within the muscularis propria and abundant vasculature. Immunostaining showed strong diffuse smooth muscle actin (SMA) positivity, weak synaptophysin expression in ~80% of tumor cells, focal CD56 positivity, and negativity for CD117 and chromogranin A—features diagnostic of gastric glomus tumor. CD56 is rarely reported and typically weak or peripheral. Because NETs more often arise in the gastric body or fundus [6], antral location and strong SMA positivity are key differentiators for diagnosing gastric glomus tumors. Pathologists should consider SMA staining when a gastric submucosal biopsy shows round cells with well-defined borders and weak synaptophysin or peripheral CD56 expression to avoid misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment for malignancy.

panels.rationale: H&E histology at ×400 shows a nest of monomorphic glomus cells surrounding vascular spaces, consistent with the glomangioma subtype of extradigital glomus tumor described in this article. The caption and in-text mention directly attribute the finding to glomus tumor histology, supporting inclusion. [raw subtype: glomangioma]
panels.attribution_text: Garcia et al. Extradigital glomus tumor: dermoscopic description and histopathological correlation.. Anais brasileiros de dermatologia 2021. doi:10.1016/j.abd.2020.11.008. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: At the center of the histological section, there is a nest consisting of glomus cells, with regular and monomorphic nuclei, surrounding vascular spaces. The adjacent dermis shows thickened collagen fibers. (Hematoxylin & eosin, ×400).
in_text_mentions: organized in single or multiple cords around vascular structures (Fig. 3). In the center of the histological section, one of these nests can be seen, showing exuberant size in relation to the others (Fig. 4). There has been no recurrence after two years of follow-up.Figure 1Angiomatous nodule on the lateral aspect of the left arm.Figure 1Figure 2Dermoscopy showed a homogeneous purplish area without structures surrounded by a whitish region, in addition to intensely purplish lagoons, standing out individually and surrounded by a pale halo (asterisks).Figure 2Figure 3Histopathology showed intrad

aces. This histopathological organization is reflected in the observed dermoscopic findings.4 In glomangiomas, the large vascular structures surrounded by delicate cell cords may stand apart and stand out individually (Fig. 4), originating the purplish lagoons described in this study. Thus, the authors believe that it is not only a dermoscopic finding associated with EGT, but it also indicates a specific subtype: glomangioma. Despite the limitation of conclusions from a single case, this new dermoscopic finding can complement the investigation and increase the accuracy of the diagnosis of EGT.

in_text_mentions: s confirmed the diagnosis of a highly undifferentiated sarcoma. After several years of being symptom‐free, the patient presented with a painful mass in the right ankle. MRI performed in November 2012 revealed multiple ovoid lesions in the distal third of the right tibia, initially raising suspicion for villonodular synovitis. Consequently, an excisional biopsy was performed in 2013. Histopathological findings were consistent with a multifocal GT. Immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin and actin, with focal positivity for H‐caldesmon and S100, confirming the diagnosis of GTs (Figure 3).

No subtype is specified in the caption or text, and no body site, age, or ethnicity is stated.

plate_findings.evidence: Tumor cells showed positive for vimentin

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is IHC of primary mandibular glomus tumor showing vimentin-positive tumor/glomus cells, supporting glomus_tumor histology finding. B: Panel B is IHC of primary glomus tumor showing MSA-positive glomus cells. C: Panel C is IHC of primary glomus tumor showing calponin-positive glomus cells. D: Panel D is IHC of primary glomus tumor showing type IV collagen positivity surrounding tumor cells, visualizing glomus cells.
panels.attribution_text: Kurohara et al. The glomus tumor resorbed bone and teeth in the mandible: a case report.. Head & face medicine 2018. doi:10.1186/s13005-018-0175-3. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemical findings of the primary glomus tumor. Tumor cells showed positive for vimentin, MSA, Calponin. The area around the tumor cells was positively stained for Type IV collagen in immunohistochemistry. a Vimentin, × 400, (b) MSA, × 400, (c) Calponin, × 400, (d) Type IV collagen, × 400

in_text_mentions: uding en bloc antrectomy and segment IVb liver with Billroth II gastrojejunostomy reconstruction. The tumor was noted to be well-encapsulated clinically and pathologically. The gross specimen (Figure 2A) showed an 11x10 x 8 cm mass involving the liver parenchyma with 90% tumor necrosis. The histology (Figure 2B) demonstrated round, epithelioid, and spindle tumor cells arranged in an organoid pattern. There is a prominent vasculature. The immunostain workup showed the tumor cells were positive for synaptophysin but negative for cytokeratin AE1/AE3/CAM5.2, chromogranin, INSMS1, GATA3, inhibin, c

six variants of unknown significance (ATM G3029D, AXIN1 V517I, KDR S1307G, NOTCH2 R1911H, RAD51B H95R, WHSC1 H528N). The MIR143-NOTCH2 fusion involved a 3’ rearrangement breakpoint in intron 26 of NOTCH2 and included exons 27-34 of NOTCH2. The fusion was reported in 389 read pairs. Additional IHC studies were performed showing the tumor cell was positive for smooth muscle actin (Figure 2C), collagen IV (Figure 2D), and smooth muscle myosin. The presence of MIR143-NOTCH2 rearrangement, together with supportive IHC and morphological features, confirmed the diagnosis of a malignant glomus tumor.

in_text_mentions: Both plain radiography and ultrasonography of the first digit of her left foot did not characterize any pathological finding. Magnetic resonance imaging of her left hallux demonstrated the presence of a subungual solid, well-delimited nodule with hyposignal and homogeneous contrast uptake at T1-weighted-image (Figure 1). Such findings suggested the diagnosis of a glomus tumor, confirmed by histopathological analysis of surgical specimen following the surgical removal of the lesion (Figure 2). Complete symptoms resolution was observed after the surgical intervention.

in_text_mentions: Histologically, the tumors were located in the gastric submucosa or muscularis and composed of glomus cells surrounding capillaries (Figure 2). Some tumors were well circumscribed (Figure 3), and the others had unclear boundaries. The glomus cells were small, uniform, and round without nuclear pleomorphism, mitotic figures, or necrosis (Figure 4). The stroma showed hyalinization or myxoid changes in some patients and ossification in one patient (Figure 5). Sporadic mast cells could be seen in the stroma. In many tumors, dilated blood vessels and/or lymphatic vessels were visible in the surroun

Most gastric neoplasms can be diagnosed according to these histological manifestations. In our study, thirteen cases were solid glomus tumors (Figure 2), and three cases were glomangiomas. Another five cases were both (Figure 3). No cases involved glomangiomyoma. Both vimentin and SMA were diffusely positive, and both H-caldesmon and calponin were partially positive. Three cases were positive for Syn.

panels.rationale: Single-panel fine-needle biopsy cytology image from the thigh mass in a case report titled 'Extradigital Glomus Tumor of Thigh.' The smear shows a cohesive sheet of uniform small round-to-polygonal cells with scanty cytoplasm, indistinct borders and round nuclei with homogeneous chromatin, matching the glomus-cell morphology in the caption and the vocabulary finding of perivascular/round glomus cells on histology. The article title and prior triage confirm glomus tumor; the TLE-1 positivity suspicious for synovial sarcoma was a diagnostic red herring that prompted excision, not the diagnosis of the biopsied lesion. Extradigital location is a recognized less common form, hence variant typicality. No skin, ethnicity, age or stage information is stated. [raw subtype: extradigital]

in_text_mentions: go and the mass gradually increased in size during this period. The pain was moderate with a visual analogue score (VAS) 6 out of 10. Further examination with Computerized Tomography (CT) revealed a 15 × 10 mm mass in subcutaneous fat tissue. Fine needle biopsy was performed and the aspirate exhibited groups of cohesive, uniform, small, round-to-polygonal cells with scanty cytoplasm, indistinct cell borders, and round nucleus with homogeneous chromatin (Figure 1). Cells were stained with TLE-1 and this was suspicious of synovial sarcoma. Therefore lesion is excised with clear surgical margins.

panels.figure_caption: Microscopic features of an extradigital glomus tumor Low (A) and higher (B, C, and D) magnification views of the pathology findings of a GET that was located on the flexor wrist of a 59-year-old woman’s right extremity. The excisional tissue specimen, using a 3-millimeter punch biopsy tool, showed nodular aggregates (black arrows) consisting of solid sheets of basophilic, uniform-appearing, glomus cells (black triangles) in the dermis (hematoxylin and eosin: A, x4; B, x10; C, x20; and D, x40).
in_text_mentions: n-absorbable sutures. Microscopic examination of the tissue specimen showed compact hyperkeratosis and mild acanthosis that correlated with the normal thickness of the skin at this location. In the dermis, there were large nodular aggregates of benign-appearing cells. The basophilic tumor consisted of solid sheets of uniform-appearing glomus cells; since the predominant component of the tumor was glomus cells with poor vasculature and sparse smooth muscle, it was classified as a glomus tumor of the solid type. In the sections examined, the neoplasm appeared to be completely removed (Figure 2).

panels.figure_caption: Histological architecture of glomus tumor. This H&E stain under 200x magnification demonstrates a dense proliferation of round glomus cells with scant eosinophilic cytoplasm and indistinct cell borders. The tumor cells are arranged in solid sheets surrounding dilated vascular spaces, which are lined by a thin endothelial layer. The overall architecture exhibits a well-organized lobular growth pattern, which is a recognized characteristic of glomangiomas.
in_text_mentions: all, branching vascular channels, surrounded by flattened and elongated cells characteristic of endothelial cells (Figure 2). in_text_mentions: ter surgery, but at 2-month followup he complained of gradual recurrence of local tenderness at the site of the excision. Three months later, the patient had a small palpable nodule and complete recurrence of his symptoms. Under local anesthesia, a very wide excision including the previous scar (with approximately 1 cm margin around the scar) was performed. Histological examination revealed glomus tumor with solid, angiomatoid, and angiomyomatous features (Figure 3). The margins of the excision were reported as free of lesion. The patient remains without any symptoms nine months after surgery.

panels.figure_caption: (a) High-magnification hematoxylin (×100) and eosin stained section that demonstrates a fragment of smooth muscle containing infiltrating uniform cells arranged around blood vessels (arrows) and (b) positive immunohistochemical stain for actin which are supportive of a diagnosis of gastric glomus tumor.
in_text_mentions: Initial interpretation of axial CT dataset did not report a gastric mass, presumedly related to the size of the lesion. Multiplanar reconstructions, however, did reveal a 1.7 cm well marginated solitary markedly enhancing mass in the gastric antrum (Figure 1). Retrospectively, the mass was found on axial CT images to display dense homogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase which persisted to the delayed phase (Figure 2). Portal vein and SMV were patent. SMA and celiac axis were unremarkable. No adenopathy was identified. Biopsy results reported a glomus tumor of the stomach (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histological section from a case report titled 'Indeterminate malignant potential glomus tumor of the esophagus.' The caption and in-text describe the tumor divided into nests by fibrous and smooth muscle septa with abundant dilated vascular spaces and solid sheets/nests of round uniform cells, which is the classic perivascular glomus cell histology of glomus tumor. It is a real patient image, not a diagram/control/other disease. Attribution to glomus_tumor is directly supported by the article title and panel-specific caption; body site esophagus comes from the article title. No skin is shown. Age and ethnicity are not stated. [raw subtype: indeterminate malignant potential]

panels.figure_caption: Histological sections show the tumor divided into nests by fibrous and smooth muscle septa, with abundant dilated vascular spaces within the tumor nests.
in_text_mentions: Macroscopic examination revealed an irregular, gray-red mass measuring 4 cm × 3 cm × 2.5 cm, partially encapsulated, with a solid gray-red cut surface and areas of hemorrhage, Fig. 2. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of solid sheets and nests of round, uniform cells with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm, Fig. 3. No mitotic figures were observed, and numerous small blood vessels were present, along with regions of hemorrhage, Fig. 4.

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histology (×100) of the ultrasound-guided biopsy from the reported extradigital glomus tumor of the thigh. The caption and in-text describe classic glomus tumor morphology: uniform small round glomus cells in sheets surrounding blood vessels with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, well-defined borders, and central round nuclei without mitotic figures or necrosis, and the in-text explicitly links these findings to the diagnosis of glomus tumor (GT of uncertain malignant potential) shown in Figure 3. Real patient image, clear quality, no third-party indication, no annotations. [raw subtype: extradigital intramuscular glomus tumor of uncertain malignant potential]
panels.attribution_text: Dai et al. Application of contrast-enhanced ultrasound for extradigital glomus tumor in the thigh: a case report.. Frontiers in oncology 2025. doi:10.3389/fonc.2025.1645052. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histological examination at ×100 objective (H&E stain) showing monotonous small round cells arranged in sheets surrounding vascular channels. The tumor cells demonstrated pale eosinophilic cytoplasm with well-defined cell borders, containing centrally located round nuclei exhibiting homogeneous chromatin patterns. Mitotic figures were conspicuously absent.
in_text_mentions: Thereafter, an ultrasound-guided biopsy of the mass was performed. Histopathology revealed that the tumor cells exhibited uniform morphology, with weakly eosinophilic cytoplasm and rich vasculature. No evidence of mitotic figure or necrosis was seen. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity with SMA and Ki-67(<5%), vessel positivity with CD31 and CD34, while negative for S-100, Melanoma, CgA or TFE3. These findings were compatible with the diagnosis of GT( Figure 3 ). Due to the mass being located within the striated muscle, the pathological diagnosis was GT of uncertain malignant potential.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Low-power H&E of the patient's biopsy (article: glomus tumor of the lower extremity) showing a circumscribed lesion with fibrous capsule, dilated vessels marked by arrows, hemorrhage, and nested/sheeted tumor cell aggregates—classic glomus tumor histology from a real human patient; consistent with prior caption triage 'keep'. B: High-power H&E of the same patient biopsy showing monomorphic small round glomus cells with distinct borders, central round-to-oval nuclei, and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm—classic glomus tumor cytology; no other disease or third-party material indicated.
panels.attribution_text: Nazemi et al. Glomus Tumor of the Lower Extremity Previously Misdiagnosed as Complex Regional Pain Syndrome in Close Proximity to a Myxofibrosarcoma: A Case Report.. panels.figure_caption: A, Image showing a circumscribed glomus tumor with a fibrous capsule, dilated vessels (arrows), hemorrhage, and nests/sheets of tumor cells separated by fibrous bands. B, Image showing uniform small round cells with distinct cell borders, centrally placed round-to-oval nuclei with relatively coarse chromatin, and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Hematoxylin and eosin staining.
in_text_mentions: Histologic sections of the biopsy from the previously diagnosed “CRPS” showed capillaries surrounded by a nested and cord arrangement of small round cells with distinct cell borders, central round-to-oval nuclei with relatively coarse chromatin, and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, which strongly expressed smooth muscle actin, calponin, and vimentin, with no expression of S100, chromogranin, synaptophysin, or pancytokeratin, consistent with glomus tumor (Figures 4 and 5).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel a is an H&E-stained patient biopsy specimen from an esophageal glomus tumor, showing the typical glomus cell proliferation and supporting the diagnosis. b: Panel b is an immunohistochemical stain of the same patient's glomus tumor, showing diffuse alpha-smooth muscle actin positivity, which supports the glomus tumor diagnosis.
panels.attribution_text: Matsumoto et al. Thoracoscopic enucleation of an esophageal glomus tumor in the prone position: a case report and literature review.. Surgical case reports 2024. doi:10.1186/s40792-024-01934-6. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Pathologic diagnosis of EUS–FNA specimens. a HE staining (×200). b Immunohistochemical staining for alpha-smooth muscle actin (×200)
in_text_mentions: oliferation of atypical cells with foci of hyalinized and fibrous stroma. Atypical cells were small round to spindled shape with increased chromatin, chromatin granularity, and irregular nuclei (Fig. 2a). Mitotic activity was not detected. Immunohistochemical staining revealed that the tumor was positive for alpha-smooth muscle actin (Fig. 2b), but negative for CD34, desmin, keratin 18, S-100 protein, melan A, c-kit, and STAT6. Therefore, he was diagnosed with esophageal GT. Based on the tumor size, histological characteristics, and patient’s physical status, tumor resection by a minimally inv

ped tumor cells with atypical round nuclei and eosinophilic to pallid cytoplasm. Mitosis or vascular invasion was not detected. Immunohistochemical staining revealed that the tumor cells were diffusely positive for alpha-smooth muscle actin. In addition to molecules such as CD34, desmin, keratin 18, S-100 protein, melan A, c-kit, and STAT6 that were examined in the preoperative biopsy specimen, AE1/AE3, synaptophysin, and DOG1 were all negative in the resected specimen. These findings were consistent with preoperative histologic examination (Fig. 2a, b), further confirming the diagnosis of GT.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E histopathology of the shoulder glomus tumor from the case report; shows perivascular glomus cell proliferation diagnostic of glomus tumor. Real patient image, no third-party copyright. B: Higher-power H&E of the same shoulder glomus tumor showing the classic perivascular round glomus cell morphology. Real patient histopathology. C: Actin (SMA) IHC positive stain highlighting the perivascular glomus cells of the shoulder glomus tumor; supports myoid differentiation typical of glomus tumor. Real patient IHC. D: CD34 IHC positive stain of the shoulder glomus tumor highlighting the perivascular glomus cells; CD34 positivity supports glomus tumor diagnosis. Real patient IHC.

panels.body_site: Dorsal tip of the right second toe
panels.rationale: Single-panel coronal fat-suppressed T1 post-gadolinium MRI of the right foot from a case report titled 'Subungual Glomus Tumor of the Toe'. The arrowed 2.5x1.5 mm well-defined enhancing subcutaneous nodule at the dorsal tip of the second toe is the classic MRI manifestation of a subungual glomus tumor, and the in-text explicitly attributes the lesion to a glomus tumor (hemangioma listed only as a differential). It is a real human-patient diagnostic image with no third-party copyright issue; the visible finding matches the vocabulary term glomus_tumor_subungual_enhancing_lesion_mri, so no additional proposed findings are needed. [raw subtype: subungual]
panels.attribution_text: Alrayyes et al. Subungual Glomus Tumor of the Toe: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.104452. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative MRI of the second toe of the right foot in coronal view (2025). There is evidence of a small, well-defined, rounded, enhancing subcutaneous nodule measuring 2.5x1.5 mm on the dorsal aspect of the tip of the second toe in the right foot, as labeled by the arrow, suggesting a vascular lesion.
in_text_mentions: On current examination, there was focal tenderness over the distal interphalangeal region without visible swelling, hyperalgesia, or nail deformity. The overlying nail plate was intact, and neurovascular status was preserved. Given the persistent nature of symptoms and localized tenderness, a repeat MRI (1.5T, fat-suppressed T1-weighted with gadolinium) was obtained, revealing a small, well-defined, rounded, enhancing subcutaneous nodule measuring 2.5x1.5 mm on the dorsal aspect of the tip of the second toe, consistent with a vascular lesion such as a glomus tumor or hemangioma (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Single-panel immunohistochemistry image from a gastric glomus tumor case report. The caption states tumor cells positive for collagen type IV, and the in-text confirms SMA and collagen type IV positivity with negative synaptophysin, chromogranin A, S-100, CD34, CD31, CD99, cytokeratin and desmin, supporting glomus tumor attribution. The microscopic field shows sheets of round glomus cells with perivascular arrangement, consistent with solid glomus tumor histology. No annotations, scale bars or panel labels are present on the image. [raw subtype: solid]

panels.rationale: H&E histology of patient tumor showing round glomus cells in perivascular arrangement with intranuclear inclusions, caption states support diagnosis of glomangioma/glomus tumor of lower extremity. [raw subtype: glomangioma]
panels.attribution_text: Patel et al. Diagnosis and Excision of Glomangioma of the Lower Extremity.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.80458. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Intra-nuclear inclusion bodies of glomus tumor cells. A H&E stain under 600x magnification demonstrates intranuclear inclusions marked by the black arrows within the glomus cells, a feature occasionally observed in these tumors. The inclusions appear as eosinophilic or clear structures within the nuclei, causing nuclear enlargement and irregularity. These findings, along with the characteristic round glomus cells and perivascular arrangement, support the diagnosis of a glomangioma.

The tumor was often embedded within a myxoid or hyalinized stroma (Figure 3). panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histopathology (x200) from the case report of primary malignant pulmonary glomus tumor. The caption and in-text describe polymorphic tumor cells with obvious nuclear atypia and pathological nuclear division around blood vessels, matching perivascular glomus cell proliferation with malignant features. Human patient tissue of the configured target disease; no third-party indication. Malignant glomus tumor is a recognized less-common form, hence variant typicality. [raw subtype: malignant_pulmonary]

panels.figure_caption: The tumor were polymorphic with obvious nuclear atypia and pathological nuclear division. H&E stain, original magnification x200.
in_text_mentions: blood vessels. Tumor cell boundary is clear, round or polygonal, partial cell fusiform, abundant cytoplasm, acidophilic granulosis or light staining; nuclear atypia is more obvious, some have nucleoli, seen in the nucleus. Inclusion body, nuclear division (4/50HPF) (Figures 8 and 9), and see pathological nuclear division (figure). Immunohistochemical staining: swelling. Tumor cells SAM, caldesmon and vimentin (diffuse +), Syn (partial +), CD34 (blood tube +), Ki‐67 (20%), EMA, CK, CgA, S‐100, Desmin, LCA, MelanA, HMB45 both (−). Pathological diagnosis: malignant glomus tumor of the right lung.

panels.rationale: Single-panel endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) image from the case report 'A Case of Gastric Glomus Tumor Misdiagnosed as Carcinoid Tumor.' The caption and in-text describe an 18.5 x 17.5 mm lesion in the gastric wall arising from the muscularis propria, slightly hypoechoic with a heterogeneous appearance and multiple vessels within the lesion, matching the hypervascular hypoechoic nodule ultrasound finding of glomus tumor. It is a real human-patient image with no third-party copyright. Gastric location is a recognized less common (variant) form of glomus tumor. Skin tone is not assessable on ultrasound, and no age or ethnicity is stated. [raw subtype: gastric]
panels.attribution_text: Ezeh et al. A Case of Gastric Glomus Tumor Misdiagnosed as Carcinoid Tumor.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.34316. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Endosonography (EUS) showing an 18.5 x 17.5 mm lesion in the gastric wall.
in_text_mentions: The patient stated that he had a good appetite without nausea, vomiting, or other lower GI symptoms. The patient denied smoking, alcohol, or illicit drug use. All other history was non-pertinent. CT scans of the abdomen with and without contrast showed mild thickening of the gastric wall without evidence of obstruction. Endosonography showed an 18.5 x 17.5 mm lesion in the gastric wall from the muscularis propria, slightly hypoechoic with a heterogenous appearance, multiple vessels within the lesion, small area of cystic degeneration, as depicted in Figure 2.

panels.rationale: Single-panel immunohistochemical image showing synaptophysin staining of the resected gastric glomus tumor. The article title ('A Case of Gastric Glomus Tumor Misdiagnosed as Carcinoid Tumor'), the caption, and the in-text mentions (synaptophysin (+), SMA (+), calponin (+), round cells devoid of atypia) all confirm this is diagnostic pathology of the patient's gastric glomus tumor. Gastric location is a recognized less common variant of glomus tumor. [raw subtype: gastric]
panels.attribution_text: Ezeh et al. A Case of Gastric Glomus Tumor Misdiagnosed as Carcinoid Tumor.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.34316. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemical stain of synaptophysin. Tumor cells show moderate cytoplasmic stains for synaptophysin.
in_text_mentions: l gastrectomy of the distal portion of the stomach. The lesion was mildly hemorrhagic (pink-purple, polypoid, rubbery nodule along the serosa measuring 1.5 x 1.0 x 0.6 cm). Multiple biopsies were taken, and all margins and surrounding omentum were negative for tumor. They appear as round cells devoid of atypia. Surrounding LN were negative for malignant cells. Immunohistochemical stains showed chromogranin (-), synaptophysin (+), smooth muscle actin (SMA) (+), calponin (+), and Ki-67. GGT was the finalized diagnosis after histology showing positive SMA and calponin [5], as seen in Figures 3-5.

panels.rationale: The image is a real patient immunohistochemical stain (H-cadherin, Envision method) of the tumor tissue from the case report, confirmed in-text as a glomus tumor of the esophagus with uncertain malignant potential. The brown chromogen highlights round glomus cells arranged perivascularly, matching the vocabulary finding for perivascular glomus cells on histology. Esophageal location with uncertain malignant potential is a recognized less-common form, hence variant. No age, ethnicity, or skin findings are applicable or stated. [raw subtype: Esophageal glomus tumor, uncertain malignant potential]

in_text_mentions: CK (‐), smooth muscle actin (SMA) (+), S-100 protein (‐), vimentin (+), Calponin (focal +), Hcaldesmon (+), Synaptophysin (+), CD56 (+), CD117 (‐), discovered on GIST-1 (‐), CD34 (‐), Desmin (focal +), Ki-67 antigen (a marker for cell proliferation) (Ki-67) (8% positive), CD31 (vascular +), ETS-related gene (scattered +), factor VIII (‐), SRY-Box Transcription Factor 10 (‐), Fig. 5. panels.figure_caption: MRI and EUS findings of the lesion. (A) Axial T1WI demonstrates a slightly hypointense lesion in the anterior wall of the gastric antrum. (B) Axial T2WI shows a slightly hyperintense lesion. in_text_mentions: MRI in June 2023 showed a round nodule with slightly low signal intensity on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) and slightly high signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI). On dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging, the lesion demonstrated mild enhancement in the early arterial phase and marked enhancement in the late arterial phase, followed by persistent enhancement in the portal venous and delayed phases (Figure 3).

Over time, the lesion showed a gradual transition from a homogeneous hypoechoic appearance to a heterogeneous hypoechoic appearance on serial EUS (Figure 3). Given the overall imaging findings, the lesion was preoperatively diagnosed as GIST, and surgical resection was performed.

The prior caption-triage confirmed this as genuine patient radiology with no third-party copyright. No skin is visible (cross-sectional imaging), so skin_tone is null. No age or ethnicity is stated. The finding_key used is the MRI category for glomus tumor; the lesion is at the proximal phalanx rather than subungual, so a more specific proposed finding is included. Malignant glomus tumor is a recognized but uncommon form, classified as variant typicality. [raw subtype: malignant]

in_text_mentions: orphologically looked like epithelial cells, many of which showed apparent dysplasia and cell division (Fig 2c,d). This tumor was negative for CK, CD34, and TTF‐1, but positive for vimentin and actin (Fig 3). Based on these pathological findings, the final diagnosis was an adenocarcinoma in the RUL and a malignant glomus tumor in the RLL. As lymph node metastasis had not developed, no adjuvant chemotherapy or radiation therapy was administered. The patient has remained healthy and without recurrence for three years following the procedure and is currently in follow‐up at an outpatient setting.

plate_findings.evidence: Well circumscribed glomus tumor, located in the wall of the stomach (H and E ×2)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power H&E showing a well-circumscribed glomus tumor within the gastric wall, consistent with the article's gastric glomus tumor diagnosis. B: High-power H&E showing round glomus cells with characteristic nuclear and cytoplasmic features, confirming the glomus tumor histomorphology. C: IHC panel showing strong brown immunostaining of the tumor cells. Caption states S100 positivity, but the in-text reports S100 negative and smooth muscle actin positive, indicating a likely caption typo (S100 should be SMA). D: IHC panel showing negative desmin immunostain of the tumor, part of the diagnostic immunoprofile supporting glomus tumor.

in_text_mentions: examination of the gastric mass showed a well‐circumscribed 3 cm tumor composed of cohesive clusters of glomus cells containing round to oval nuclei with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, infrequent mitotic activity, and low proliferation index of 10%, as measured by Ki‐67 immunohistochemistry. The tumor cells were strongly positive for smooth muscle actin, calponin, caldesmon, and synaptophysin, and negative for CD 117, CD 34, CD 56, S 100, CK 20, and chromogranin. Excision was complete. The morphological and immunohistochemical features confirmed the diagnosis of a glomus tumor (See Figure 4A–D).

panels.rationale: Single gross photograph of an excised human specimen from a case of esophageal glomus tumor. The image shows a nodular, partially encapsulated mass with a gray-red cut surface and visible hemorrhage, directly matching the glomus_tumor_excised_reddish_tumor finding and the caption description. Disease attribution to glomus tumor is supported by the article title and in-text macroscopic description. Esophageal location and indeterminate malignant potential make the presentation atypical for this entity.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Gross specimen photograph of the surgically resected duodenal mass from the reported malignant glomus tumor case; the caption and article title directly attribute this specimen to glomus tumor, and the excised-tumor finding key applies despite the cut surface being grayish-white to light brown rather than reddish. [raw subtype: malignant] B: H&E histopathology of the duodenal glomus tumor showing the textbook perivascular glomus cell proliferation pattern; caption and in-text both confirm this is the resected human tumor from the malignant glomus tumor case report. [raw subtype: malignant] C: High-power H&E section (400×) of the same duodenal glomus tumor showing clear cytoplasm, moderate nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli, and mitotic figures; the in-text attributes these features to the tumor in Figures 3B,C, and the malignant cytologic features represent a less common (variant) form of glomus tumor. [raw subtype: malignant]

in_text_mentions: Gross examination revealed a solid mass in the duodenum, measuring 3 × 3 × 2 cm, located approximately 1 cm from the pancreas. The cut surface appeared gray-white to tan, solid, and firm (Figure 3A).

Histologically, the tumor demonstrated diffuse sheets of cells encircling proliferating vasculature. The cytoplasm was variably clear to eosinophilic. Tumor nuclei showed moderate atypia, conspicuous nucleoli, and frequent mitotic figures, including atypical mitoses. Evidence of infiltrative growth through the duodenal mucosa and muscularis propria was noted (Figures 3B,C).

panels.figure_caption: The tumor was composed of relatively uniform round cells with perivascular aggregation, surrounding branching thin-walled vessels (A, ×200, HE staining). The mesenchyma of the tumor showed mucinous degeneration and hyalinization (C, ×400, HE staining). The tumor cells appeared round nuclei, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm (B, ×400, HE staining) and sharply defined cell borders, which was enhanced by PAS staining (D, ×400). Cytological atypia and increased mitotic activity were observed locally (B, ×400, HE staining). HE, hematoxylin and eosin; PAS, periodic acid-Schiff.
in_text_mentions: in-walled vessels. The mesenchyma of the tumor showed mucinous degeneration and hyalinization. The tumor cells are composed of round nuclei, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm and sharply defined cell borders, which was enhanced by PAS staining. Slight cytological atypia was observed locally, and increased mitotic activity (the mitotic count was at 12-19 per 50 HPF) (Figure 2). The tumor revealed locally infiltrative growth pattern into all layers of the bronchus wall, and the surgical resection margin was involved by glomus tumor tissue. No metastasis was noted in the 6 lymph nodes below the carina.

The stromal component exhibited mucoid and hyaline degeneration (Figure 2A,B). The diagnosis was determined as a glomus tumor. IHC staining further confirmed tumor's smooth muscle and mesenchymal origins, with positive for vimentin (Figure 3A), smooth muscle antibody (SMA, Figure 3B), synapsin (Syn, Figure 3C), actin (Figure 3D), desmin (Figure 3E), CD34 (vascular, Figure 3F), while negative for and chromogranin A (CgA, Figure 3G). The histopathological findings in our case revealed typical features of a glomus tumor, as illustrated in Figure 2. Our findings reinforce the characteristic IHC profile observed in glomus tumors, marked by positive staining for vimentin, SMA, actin, and desmin, which underscore the tumor's smooth muscle and mesenchymal origins [31, 32, 33]. The presence of CD34 further corroborates the vascular nature of these tumors [32]. Additionally, the low Ki‐67 index supports the benign nature of the tumor, aligning with the typical profile of most glomus tumors [33].

in_text_mentions: umor, arising from the submucosa of the stomach and extending throughout all layers of the muscular propria, involving the serous surface. Histologically, the tumor was composed of sheets of glomus cells, without nuclear pleomorphism and no mitotic figures. The cells had eosinophilic and focally clear cytoplasm. The nuclei of these cells are round, with inconspicuous nucleoli. The cells contours were clear, and it was possible to identify dilated blood vessels among the cell blocks and areas of stromal hyalinization (Figure 4(a)). We could not identify vascular, lymphatic, or nervous invasion.

The immunohistochemical panel showed that the tumor cells were positive for smooth muscle actin and collagen type IV (Figure 4(b)) and negative for desmin, CD34, CD117, S-100 protein, creatin kinase, p53, chromogranin, and cytokeratins (Table 1). The proliferating marker Ki-67 was <5% confirming the low rate of mitosis in each histological field analyzed. The gastric margins are free of neoplastic compromise, but the mucosa showed erosive gastritis and positivity for Helicobacter pylori. in_text_mentions: hologic examination a revealed a circumscribed mass consisting of uniform cells in haematoxylin eosin stain (Figure 1). A negative resection margin was confirmed. The tumor cells had centrally placed nuclei and were arranged in perivascular nests. A marked hyalinization was identified in the tumoral vessel walls (Figure 2). Immunostaining for smooth muscle actin (SMA), vimentin and caldesmon was strongly positive, whereas a negative result for CKAE1/AE3, S100 and MELANA was noted. Positive CD34 loci were also identified. Based on these, the diagnosis of a glomus tumor was confirmed (Figure 3).

in_text_mentions: in the subcutaneous region of the anterior aspect of the upper extremity. The tumor presented itself as a bluish multifocal area 5–10 mm in diameter, just above biceps muscle (Figure 1). During surgery, the tumor was exposed through a short skin incision on the left upper arm (Figure 2). The operation was followed by permanent and immediate relief of pain. Histological examination showed dilated vascular area with proliferated glomus cells with a round nucleus in the wall of dilated vascular structures (Figures 3 and 4). Final diagnosis, based on the histological examination, was glomangioma.

panels.rationale: Single-panel coronal T1-weighted MRI of the right index finger showing a small lesion dorsal to the distal phalanx with low T1 signal intensity. The in-text describes the identical lesion with high T2 signal and intense homogeneous enhancement, and states the initial radiological impression based on location and radiological features was a glomus tumor — the classic MRI manifestation of a subungual glomus tumor. The article title reports the final diagnosis was clear cell sarcoma with an unusual presentation misdiagnosed as a glomus tumor, so attribution rests on the glomus-typical radiological presentation rather than pathology, which lowers confidence but does not negate that the panel visibly shows the glomus tumor manifestation. [raw subtype: subungual]

panels.body_site: subcutaneous tissue of the upper extremity (anterior upper arm above biceps)
panels.rationale: Single H&E histology detail from a human surgical specimen. Caption and in-text explicitly describe proliferated glomus cells with round nuclei in the walls of dilated vascular structures, and the article states the final histological diagnosis was glomangioma (a glomus tumor subtype), in the subcutaneous region of the upper extremity. The perivascular glomus cell proliferation around dilated vascular channels matches the vocabulary finding directly. The presentation is variant because the article frames the upper-extremity localization as rare, while the histologic pattern itself is textbook. No skin is visible, so skin_tone is null; no ethnicity or age is stated. [raw subtype: glomangioma]

in_text_mentions: in the subcutaneous region of the anterior aspect of the upper extremity. The tumor presented itself as a bluish multifocal area 5–10 mm in diameter, just above biceps muscle (Figure 1). During surgery, the tumor was exposed through a short skin incision on the left upper arm (Figure 2). The operation was followed by permanent and immediate relief of pain. Histological examination showed dilated vascular area with proliferated glomus cells with a round nucleus in the wall of dilated vascular structures (Figures 3 and 4). Final diagnosis, based on the histological examination, was glomangioma.

panels.rationale: Single-panel hematoxylin and eosin histopathology of the resected tumor from a human patient. The disease-focused title (Primary Renal Glomus Tumor of Uncertain Malignant Potential), the caption, and the in-text final diagnosis (renal glomus tumor with features suggestive of uncertain malignant potential) directly attribute the panel to glomus tumor. The solid sheets and nests of uniform round-to-oval cells with central nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and intratumoral vascular structures match the perivascular glomus-cell histology finding; only focal cytologic atypia is additionally present. This is a real patient specimen, not a diagram, control, animal model, or other-disease comparison, and it carries no third-party restriction; no annotations are overlaid. [raw subtype: primary renal, uncertain malignant potential]

in_text_mentions: Histologically, the tumor was composed of atypical glomus cell nests surrounding capillaries (Figure 3). Immunohistochemical staining revealed the tumor cells to be positive for vimentin, smooth muscle actin, and collagen type IV (Figure 4). Staining for CD34, synaptophysin, and chromogranin A revealed that they were not expressed in these tumor cells. Taken together, our analysis led to diagnosis of this lesion as a gastric GT.

panels.rationale: Single endoscopic ultrasound image; caption states 'Ultrasound image of glomus tumor' and the disease-focused article title ('Gastric Glomus Tumor') plus in-text description (3 cm well-circumscribed homogeneous prepyloric submucosal lesion in a 41-year-old female) directly attribute the panel to gastric glomus tumor. It is real patient imaging of untreated disease, so it is included; gastric location makes it a variant rather than the classic subungual presentation. [raw subtype: gastric]
panels.attribution_text: Morte et al. Gastric Glomus Tumor: An Uncommon Source for an Acute Upper GI Bleed.. Case reports in gastrointestinal medicine 2018. doi:10.1155/2018/7961981. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Ultrasound image of glomus tumor.
in_text_mentions: The patient is an otherwise healthy 41-year-old female who initially presented with a hemodynamically significant, but self-limited, upper GI bleed. She required 4 units of packed red blood cells in total for stabilization. An upper endoscopy was performed which showed an ulcerated gastric mass (Figure 1). A subsequent endoscopic ultrasound revealed a 3 cm well-circumscribed and homogeneous submucosal lesion (Figure 2). CT scan confirmed the 3.0 × 2.9 × 2.7 cm hyperenhancing, prepyloric, submucosal mass with no radiographic evidence of metastasis (Figure 3).

Arrows highlight vascular spaces within the perivascular glomus cell proliferation. [raw subtype: angiomatoid]

in_text_mentions: The diagnosis of a glomus tumor is confirmed when histology demonstrates cells with a positive expression for CD34 and smooth muscle actin [16]. Three different histologic variants have been reported, including (1) solid, with poor vasculature and scant smooth muscle component, (2) angiomatoid (glomangioma) with a predominant vascular component, and (3) glomangiomyoma with prominent vascular and smooth muscle components [17]. As seen in Figure 5, there was a prominent vascular component to our patient’s tumor.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Coronal T1 and post-contrast T1 MRI of the right shoulder showing a nodular lesion in the deltoid muscle with strong enhancement, attributed by the caption and article to a glomus tumor; real patient image of the target disease, though at an atypical intramuscular site rather than subungual. [raw subtype: intramuscular] B: Sagittal T2 MRI showing a hyperintense nodule in the right deltoid muscle, the glomus tumor lesion described in the caption and in-text; real patient image of the target disease at an intramuscular site. [raw subtype: intramuscular] C: Axial and sagittal post-contrast fat-suppressed T1 MRI showing a hyperintense, well-limited lesion in the posterior deltoid, matching the glomus tumor described in the caption and in-text; real patient image of the target disease, intramuscular location making it a variant presentation. [raw subtype: intramuscular]
panels.attribution_text: Vieira et al. Glomus Tumor: "A-Not-So-Rare" Cause of Chronic Shoulder Pain-A Case Report and Literature Review.. Case reports in orthopedics 2021. doi:10.1155/2021/6666092. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: MRI images of the right shoulder. (a) Coronal images showing a nodular formation in the deltoid muscle (yellow arrows). The lesion is hypointense in T1 (left picture), but with strong enhancement with contrast (right picture). (b) Sagittal T2 image with turbo spin echo before contrast. The lesion appears as a hyperintense nodule (yellow arrow). (c) Axial (left) and sagittal (right) T1 images with fat suppression after contrast show a hyperintense well-limited lesion in the posterior deltoid (yellow arrows).
in_text_mentions: Plain radiographs were normal (Figure 1). Ultrasonography of the right shoulder denoted a hypoechoic nodular formation in the point of tenderness, measuring 13 mm (Figure 2). Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) confirmed the presence of a well-limited oval-shaped mass located in the posterior fibers of the right deltoid muscle, measuring 25 × 10 × 6 mm, which was hypointense in T1 and hyperintense in T2-weighted images and exhibited strong enhancement with contrast (Figures 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real patient upper-gastrointestinal endoscopy from the reported gastric glomus tumor case, showing the index 30 mm well-circumscribed soft submucosal tumor with normal overlying mucosa in the anterior wall of the gastric antrum. Disease attribution rests on the case title plus this captioned manifestation in the same patient. No controlled-vocabulary finding_key describes an endoscopic gastric submucosal mass, so the visible manifestation is recorded in proposed_findings; gastric location is a less common (variant) presentation of glomus tumor. B: Same patient's endoscopic ultrasonography: a well-demarcated hypoechoic mass confined to the third and fourth layers of the gastric wall, with CT dense homogeneous enhancement indicating hypervascularity, matching the hypervascular hypoechoic nodule ultrasound finding of glomus tumor. The gastric location is a recognized but uncommon (variant) presentation rather than the classic subungual form.

in_text_mentions: muscle cells or fibrous bands. The tumor ulcerated the overlying mucosa, involved mucosa, submucosa, and muscularis propria, and extended to the serosa. The tumor nodules showed a relatively solid pattern with pericytoma-like gaping capillary vessels. Cytoplasmic clearing was noted. The tumor cells showed sharply defined cell membranes and centrally located round, uniform nuclei with delicate chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli with focal areas of spindled cells. Areas of coagulative necrosis were observed. Mitotic activity was approximately 4-5/50 high-power field (HPF) (Figures 2(a)–2(f)).

D: Histology panel shows solid malignant glomus tumor growth with epithelioid cells, consistent with the article's malignant glomus tumor diagnosis. [raw subtype: malignant] E: Low-magnification histology panel shows venous vascular invasion and infiltration into adipose and striated muscle in malignant glomus tumor. [raw subtype: malignant] F: Histology panel shows venous vascular tumor invasion, a feature of malignant glomus tumor. [raw subtype: malignant]
panels.attribution_text: Arregui et al. Complete response to encorafenib plus binimetinib in a <i>BRAF V600E</i>-mutant metastasic malignant glomus tumor.. Oncotarget 2024. doi:10.18632/oncotarget.28654. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Pathology images (A–D). Immunohistochemistry staining. Histologically, a well-demarcated, unencapsulated, multinodular, densely cellular neoplasm is observed, that grows forming large nodules composed of cells of epithelioid morphology with well-demarcated, broad, eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm, with nuclei with fine chromatin, some of them with presence of eosinophilic nucleolus growing in subcutaneous cellular adipose tissue with images of tumor necrosis and vascular invasion. There are 12 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. The tumor is associated with vascular structures with large areas of blood extravasation and hemosiderophages. The tumor infiltrates the included striated muscle tissue and the surgical resection margin. Transition is identified between well-differentiated low-grade areas (benign glomus tumor) and the predominant high-grade tumor. Immunohistochemical profile was: Actin ML (focal), Actin HHF35, H-caldesmon and Collagen IV (characteristic pericellular and diffuse pattern), p16 (predominantly cytoplasmic) positive; CKAE1-AE3, CK19, Myogenin, Desmin, S100, HMB45, MELAN-A, CD34, CD31, ERG, FACTORVIII, CD138, EMA, CD68, TFE3, D2-40 and HHV8 negative. (A) Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) X 10. Peripheral focus of benign glomus tumor. (B) HE X 10. Peripheral focus of benign glomus (larger diameter). (C) IHC X 10. Patchy positive staining for ML-Actin. (D) HE X 20. Solid tumor growth on a collagenous stroma. The cells are of epithelioid morphology with clear or amphophilic cytoplasm very well demarcated and enlarged oval nuclei with fine chromatin. (E) HE X 5. Low magnification, in the periphery of the tumor two images of venous vascular invasion and infiltration of the included adipose and striated muscle tissue are observed. (F) HE X 20. Venous vascular tumor invasion.
in_text_mentions: New biopsy attempts were unsuccessful. Surgical excision showed a tumor affecting the wall musculature and presenting an infiltrative, friable, and vascularized appearance, compatible with a diagnosis of malignant glomus tumor. The patient was referred to our hospital, a national reference center for sarcoma, for evaluation of radical surgery. The pathological review of the surgical specimen confirmed the diagnosis of GT (Figure 2).

source_variant.figure_caption: Pathology images (A–D). Immunohistochemistry staining. Histologically, a well-demarcated, unencapsulated, multinodular, densely cellular neoplasm is observed, that grows forming large nodules composed of cells of epithelioid morphology with well-demarcated, broad, eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm, with nuclei with fine chromatin, some of them with presence of eosinophilic nucleolus growing in subcutaneous cellular adipose tissue with images of tumor necrosis and vascular invasion. There are 12 mitoses per 10 high-power fields. The tumor is associated with vascular structures with large areas of blood extravasation and hemosiderophages. The tumor infiltrates the included striated muscle tissue and the surgical resection margin. Transition is identified between well-differentiated low-grade areas (benign glomus tumor) and the predominant high-grade tumor. Immunohistochemical profile was: Actin ML (focal), Actin HHF35, H-caldesmon and Collagen IV (characteristic pericellular and diffuse pattern), p16 (predominantly cytoplasmic) positive; CKAE1-AE3, CK19, Myogenin, Desmin, S100, HMB45, MELAN-A, CD34, CD31, ERG, FACTORVIII, CD138, EMA, CD68, TFE3, D2-40 and HHV8 negative. (A) Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) X 10. Peripheral focus of benign glomus tumor. (B) HE X 10. Peripheral focus of benign glomus (larger diameter). (C) IHC X 10. Patchy positive staining for ML-Actin. (D) HE X 20. Solid tumor growth on a collagenous stroma. The cells are of epithelioid morphology with clear or amphophilic cytoplasm very well demarcated and enlarged oval nuclei with fine chromatin. (E) HE X 5. Low magnification, in the periphery of the tumor two images of venous vascular invasion and infiltration of the included adipose and striated muscle tissue are observed. (F) HE X 20. Venous vascular tumor invasion.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Panel a H&E x40 of gastric glomangioma showing submucosal glomus cells around dilated vessels, consistent with glomus tumor perivascular glomus cells. b: Panel b H&E x100 shows uniform round glomus cells with sharply defined borders arranged around vessels, classic glomus tumor histology. c: Panel c SMA IHC x100 shows diffuse SMA positivity, consistent with glomus tumor phenotype; tumor cells visually present, SMA term not in glomus_tumor vocabulary so proposed. d: Panel d synaptophysin IHC x100 of same gastric glomangioma showing tumor cells with strong synaptophysin expression, described as potential diagnostic pitfall mimicking neuroendocrine tumors; atypical immunophenotype, synaptophysin term proposed as not in vocabulary.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological and immunohistochemical features of gastric glomangioma. (a) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E, ×40): a submucosal proliferative tumor lesion composed of small clusters of glomus cells surrounding dilated, erythrocyte-filled vessels (*), resembling cavernous hemangioma-like structures. (b) H&E (×100): the tumor consists of uniform, small, round glomus cells with monotonous round nuclei, vesicular chromatin, and amphophilic to lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm. These cells exhibited sharply defined borders (→) and were arranged in clusters surrounding dilated vascular structures (*). (c) Smooth muscle actin {SMA} immunohistochemistry {IHC} (×100): diffuse SMA positivity, consistent with glomus tumor phenotype. (d) Synaptophysin IHC (×100): strong synaptophysin expression, a potential diagnostic pitfall mimicking neuroendocrine tumors.
in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination revealed a well-circumscribed submucosal lesion composed of round glomus cells arranged around dilated, erythrocyte-filled vascular channels, resembling cavernous hemangioma-like structures. The tumor showed monotonous architecture with amphophilic to lightly eosinophilic cytoplasm and vesicular chromatin (Figures 4a-4d). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated positivity for smooth muscle actin (SMA), vimentin, and calponin, with negativity for cluster of differentiation 117 (CD117), Discovered on GIST-1 (DOG1), desmin, and S-100 (Table 2, Figures 4a-4d).
